newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sick pay cuts creep in outside German metal sector.
newsitem.headline: Sick pay cuts creep in outside German metal sector.

text.p: Protests by hundreds of thousands of German metal workers against possible cuts to sick pay this week overshadow the fact that firms in other sectors are already moving ahead with plans to implement the cuts.
German chemical employers and the IG Chemie trade union said after a meeting in Wiesbaden on Friday that they would be including talks on sick pay in the 1997 wage round.

The discussions were demanded by IG Chemie after chemicals group BASF AG earlier this month said it would be implementing a new law allowing it to cut sick pay from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
BASF's move unleashed protests involving some 13,000 workers, with worker representatives threatening further action if the company did not back down.

But in a joint statement that contained none of the vitriol which followed the collapse of talks in the metal and engineering sector earlier this week, IG Chemie and chemical employers said on Friday they planned to restart negotiations on November 19.
Sources close to the two sides, which pride themselves on their ability to hammer out wage deals quickly, said the would be seeking "innovative ways" around the problem.
But discussions in the chemical sector start as large banking and construction employers have already confirmed they will implement the law.

The ZDB national employers federation for the German construction industry, which employs some 1.4 million workers, said on Thursday that it was recommending that its member firms implement the cut immediately.

ZDB president Fritz Eichbauer said that the cuts could be put into effect because wage contracts for construction workers did not expressly state that they were entitled to sick payments at 100 percent of salary.

The German IG Bau construction trade union, currently locked in a separate fight with employers to bring east German wage levels closer to those in the west of the country, accepts that the reductions will go ahead.
"We must accept it. Contracts for building workers do not rule out the cuts," an IG Bau spokesman said on Friday, reiterating an earlier position.

IG Metall, Germany's most powerful trade union with some three million members, has in the last month been able to capitalise on the legal uncertainty surrounding wage contracts in the metal and engineering sectors.
It argues that the vast majority of its members have contracts with clauses specifically guaranteeing sick payments at 100 percent of salary and that the new law cannot override these contracts.

The Gesamtmetall employers federation -- while strongly disagreeing with that interpretation -- has so far been unable to persuade its members to implement the new law because of the huge sense of injustice felt by metal workers at the cuts.
German banks including Germany's largest, Deutsche Bank, and Commerzbank AG, have both said they would also be seeking to put the cuts into effect from the start of next month.
White-collar union DAG earlier this month threatened industrial action if the reductions were made and has said that employee feeling against the law is running high.
But banking sector wage contracts, like those in the construction industry, do not enshrine immediate sick payments at 100 percent of salary.

There is greater chance for conflict in the insurance sector, where the DAG union says most contracts do guarantee sick payments at the full rate. No major insurance companies have so far announced plans to implement the cuts, however.
